newsitem.title: INDIA: India blocks Singapore Airlines project.
newsitem.headline: India blocks Singapore Airlines project.

text.p: India has barred foreign airlines from taking equity stakes in the aviation sector, blocking a controversial proposed investment by Singapore Airlines Ltd, the Civil Aviation Ministry said on Wednesday.

The decision, taken by Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's cabinet late on Tuesday, ruled out the proposed $600 million tie-up between Singapore Airlines Ltd (SIA) and India's Tata group, industry officials said.

It also appeared to mark a victory for Civil Aviation Minister C.M. Ibrahim, who has fought a high-profile campaign to protect the state-owned airlines -- Indian Airlines on domestic routes and Air-India on international routes -- from foreign competition.
In February 1995, SIA and Tata Industries Ltd submitted their proposal to launch a joint airline. The Tatas were planning to hold a 60 percent stake, with SIA owning the rest.
The proposal has since languished in the government, ensnared in a high-stakes battle over whether to permit foreign investment in the civil aviation sector.
Tata Industries vice-president S. Ramakrishnan, who is in charge of the Tata-SIA project, called the decision a setback.
"We can only say we are very disappointed," Ramakrishnan told Reuters in Bombay.
"It's a bit too early to say what the next step will be." But he did not rule out the possibility of salvaging the deal in some form.

A Civil Aviation Ministry spokeswoman said the cabinet also upheld a rule, set in January, limiting foreign firms which are not airlines to 40 percent equity stakes in domestic airlines. Non-resident Indians can hold stakes of up to 100 percent.
"The cabinet in its meeting yesterday said foreign investment is welcome in the domestic civil aviation sector," the spokeswoman said.
"However, equity from foreign airlines directly or indirectly has not been recommended," she said, adding that the recommendation amounted to a prohibition.
Foreign investors, whether or not they are airlines, which currently hold stakes in Indian airlines will have to conform to the rules, she said.
Gulf Air and Kuwait Airways each have 20 percent stakes, valued at $4.0 million, in India's Jet Airways.
India began opening its aviation sector as part of an economic liberalisation programme launched under then-prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao in 1991.
